title: Low Libido, No Pregnancy, Tall Young Man / Testosterone Would Switch Off His Sperm

blocks.text: Low Libido, No Pregnancy, Tall Young Man / Testosterone Would Switch Off His Sperm

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-28 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Testosterone therapy in men with hypogonadism (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:1715) · Related AMaC: AMaC gynaecomastia and premature ovarian insufficiency stations; this one tests primary testicular failure

Dear Doctor, a 31-year-old joiner. He and his partner have tried for a baby for 18 months without success. He has low libido and tiredness. He is tall with sparse facial hair. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Low libido, tiredness and infertility in a tall man with small testes is hypogonadism, and the pattern of the pituitary hormones tells you where it comes from. The station turns on not giving testosterone to a man who wants children.

The Examiner Trap. He asks for testosterone to feel better. Candidates agree, which would suppress sperm production. Pass: two morning testosterone levels, LH and FSH, karyotype, fertility first. Fail: testosterone started.

rows: Ask about libido, erections, energy, the baby attempts, puberty, headaches, vision, drugs and infections.
"How are your libido and erections? How long have you tried for a baby? Any headaches or vision problems? Any drugs?"
Libido; erections; puberty; testicular history; headaches; vision; opioids; mumps; family history; fertility.
Examine the build, hair, breasts and testes, and test the visual fields.
"May I check your height, hair and chest, examine your testes and test your vision? Tell me if anything hurts."
Height; arm span; hair; breasts; ask for testes size and penis findings; visual fields; cover him.
Explain what the tests will show, why testosterone could harm his fertility, and what happens next.
"I need blood tests on two mornings and a chromosome test. Testosterone would lower your sperm count, so I'd rather not start it now."
Testosterone twice; LH and FSH; karyotype; semen; fertility team; sperm banking; follow-up.
No introduction or consent; examines the testes without asking; leaves him exposed.
Introduces self, asks consent, offers a chaperone before the genital examination, covers him and thanks him.
Also acknowledges how hard it is to talk about libido and fertility.
Asks about libido only; omits fertility, puberty, headaches or drugs.
Asks libido, erections, the baby attempts, puberty, testicular history, headaches, vision and opioids.
Also asks about mumps, undescended testes, family history and alcohol.
Omits the testes or visual fields; reports signs that are absent.
Finds a tall man with sparse hair, small firm testes and normal visual fields.
Also asks for testis size by orchidometer and looks for breast enlargement.
Calls it stress or low mood.
Hypogonadism, probably testicular (primary) in cause, with infertility.
Also names Klinefelter syndrome, pituitary disease, opioids and obesity as causes.
Asks for fasting morning total testosterone on two mornings, LH and FSH, prolactin, a karyotype if the testes are small, and a semen analysis.
Also asks for biotin to be stopped for at least 72 hours before LH and FSH, and for a repeat semen analysis a few weeks later.
Starts testosterone at once, or says nothing about fertility.
Says testosterone suppresses sperm production, defers it, refers to a fertility team, and gives return advice for headaches or vision change.
Also explains that if the semen contains no sperm, the fertility team can discuss surgical sperm retrieval.
Brushes aside his fear of never being a father.
Asks what worries him, acknowledges it and explains that specialist treatment may still help.
Also discusses his partner and how they are coping.
Tells him what to do with no choices.
Explains the tests, the fertility referral and later options, and asks his view.
Records his view, gives a written plan and a dated review.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 31-year-old joiner. You are embarrassed, practical and desperate to be a father.
Opening line: "We've been trying for a baby for a year and a half and nothing's happening. I've also got no interest in sex and I'm knackered all the time."
Volunteered: your partner is 29 and has had tests that were fine. You were always the tallest at school.

Only if asked: you shave about twice a week. Erections are weak. No headaches or vision trouble. No drugs. No mumps that you know of. You do not smoke and drink a few pints at weekends. No other medicines and no allergies. No recent travel. No family history of infertility or hormone problems.
Only if asked about puberty: it was a bit late, and your voice broke late.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you are not a real man and will lose your partner. Say: "She deserves someone who can give her a family."
Your questions, in your own words: "Can you give me testosterone?" "Will I be able to have children?" "Why is it me?"
How you react: if told no with no reason, you are hurt. If listened to and given a plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: tall; respiratory rate 14; pulse 70 regular; blood pressure 124/76; temperature 36.6 °C. Sparse facial and body hair. Mild breast enlargement. Testicular findings are not examined on the role-player: the examiner gives them only if the candidate asks, explains the indication, and says consent and a chaperone would be arranged. Both testes small and firm. Visual fields normal.
Results, only when requested: fasting morning total testosterone low on two mornings; LH and FSH raised; prolactin normal. Testes about 3 mL each. Semen: no sperm. Karyotype: 47,XXY.

Question ladder: 1. How do you diagnose hypogonadism? (D) 2. What do high LH and FSH tell you? (D) 3. Why check the karyotype? (E) 4. Should he have testosterone now? (E) 5. How do you monitor testosterone later? (E)

Curveballs: He asks to start it anyway: no, it would suppress sperm; the fertility team first. He asks about sperm banking: banking ejaculate will not help if the semen has no sperm; the fertility team can discuss surgical sperm retrieval. He reports new headaches and blurred vision: urgent pituitary imaging and visual fields.
Introduces self, asks consent and offers a chaperone when asking for the testicular findings (G)
Asks about the baby attempts, puberty, headaches and drugs (C)
Examines the chest and visual fields and asks for the testicular findings (A)
Finds sparse hair and uses the testicular findings supplied (small, firm) (B)
Names hypogonadism, probably primary, with infertility (D)
Requests fasting morning testosterone on two mornings, LH and FSH (E)
Requests a karyotype because the testes are small (E)
Says testosterone suppresses sperm production and refers to a fertility team (E)
Gives return advice for headaches and vision change (E)
Asks what worries him and addresses his fear (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Drop your trousers. [R1 Fail] Any stress? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Does not ask for the testicular findings.) [R3 Fail] Low mood. [R4 Fail] One testosterone level. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: I'll start testosterone gel. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a year. [R8 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent, no chaperone, the testicular findings not sought, and testosterone given to a man who wants children.
Pass performance

CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine your chest and vision? Tell me if anything hurts. I'd also like to know the testicular findings, because they show where the low testosterone comes from; I'd ask your consent and have a chaperone. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: How long have you tried for a baby? When did puberty happen? Any headaches or vision problems? Any drugs? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Eighteen months. Late. No headaches. No drugs.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, asks the examiner for the testicular findings, then covers him and thanks him.) Sparse hair, normal visual fields and, as given, small firm testes. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I think you have low testosterone from the testes, which also explains the fertility problem. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I need fasting morning testosterone on two mornings, LH and FSH, prolactin, a chromosome test and a semen test. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Testosterone would lower your sperm count, so I'd refer you to the fertility team first. Come back urgently with headaches or vision change. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: That I'm not a real man.
CANDIDATE: That is a fair fear; this is a medical condition, and there are options. [R7 Pass] Shall we do the first blood test now? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Gave the plan and protected his fertility. Did not name other causes, biotin, sperm retrieval or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? Many men find this hard to discuss. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any mumps, undescended testes or alcohol? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines; asks for the testicular findings.) Mild breast enlargement; I'd ask the examiner for the testis size by orchidometer. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Klinefelter syndrome fits; pituitary disease, opioids and obesity are other causes. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Please stop any biotin supplement for at least 72 hours before the LH and FSH test, and we will repeat the semen test in a few weeks. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: If the semen shows no sperm, the fertility team can talk to you about retrieving sperm from the testes, and that is worth discussing early. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Is your partner coming to the next visit? [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, other causes, orchidometer, biotin, sperm retrieval and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about puberty and fertility. They point to a testicular cause.
R4: Calling it stress. Small testes, sparse hair and infertility are hypogonadism.
R5: Relying on one random level. Two fasting morning levels are needed, with LH and FSH.
R6: Starting testosterone. It would lower his sperm production.
"Can I ask about puberty and what you have tried for a baby?"
"Small testes and low testosterone point to a testicular cause."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

Endocrine Society 2018: diagnose hypogonadism with symptoms or signs plus consistently low total or free testosterone. Measure fasting morning total testosterone on two separate mornings; do not screen the general population. Measure LH and FSH to separate primary from secondary causes; stop biotin 72 hours before.

Secondary causes: check prolactin, iron studies; consider pituitary tests and MRI if testosterone is very low, with panhypopituitarism, persistent hyperprolactinaemia or mass effect. If primary hypogonadism has no obvious cause, obtain a karyotype for Klinefelter syndrome, especially if the testes are under 6 mL.

Testosterone therapy suppresses spermatogenesis; near-term fertility plans are a contraindication. Men with sperm in the semen who may want children later can consider sperm banking; if there is none, the fertility team can discuss surgical sperm retrieval.
THINK: Tall, small testes, infertile: primary hypogonadism.
SAY: "Testosterone would lower your sperm count."
DO: Consent and chaperone; ask for testes findings; visual fields.
NUMBERS: Karyotype in unexplained primary hypogonadism, especially testes under 6 mL (Endocrine Society).
TRAP: Starting testosterone.
FINISH: Two morning levels, LH/FSH, karyotype, fertility team.

Bhasin S et al. Testosterone therapy in men with hypogonadism: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:1715. https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2018-00229 Supports: Diagnosis on two fasting morning levels, LH and FSH, biotin, karyotype below 6 mL, avoiding testosterone when fertility is planned, semen analysis.
